recommendation.recommendation: Apply organic manure (compost or well‑decomposed farmyard manure) to increase soil organic carbon.
recommendation.justification: Soil analysis shows a low organic carbon level despite an overall excellent soil health score (92) and optimal pH, nitrogen, and texture for mango. Mango trees require high organic carbon to sustain the high water and nutrient demand during fruiting. Improving organic matter will boost soil structure, water‑holding capacity, and nutrient availability, reinforcing the already favorable NDVI and weather conditions and mitigating the identified risk of low organic carbon.
actions: Source high‑quality compost or well‑decomposed farmyard manure (minimum C:N ratio ~12:1).
Apply 5–7 tonnes per hectare (≈0.5–0.7 kg m⁻²) evenly over the mango orchard, focusing on the root zone (0–30 cm depth).
Incorporate the manure into the topsoil using a rotavator or manual spading to ensure good contact with soil.
Water the treated area with the existing drip‑irrigation system immediately after incorporation to activate microbial activity.
Record the amount applied, date, and weather conditions in the farm log.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Increase in soil organic carbon to within the mango optimal range within 2–3 months, leading to improved water retention, nutrient supply, and a potential 5‑10 % rise in fruit yield and marketable quality.
monitoring_plan: Soil organic carbon test: collect samples 2 weeks after application and again at 8 weeks; compare to baseline (target ≥ 2.5 %).
Visual crop check: weekly inspection for leaf vigor, fruit set, and any signs of nutrient deficiency.
NDVI review: request updated satellite imagery 30 days post‑application; aim to maintain NDVI ≥ 0.75.
Irrigation check: ensure drip lines remain functional and adjust frequency if soil moisture drops below field capacity.
Record market price trends monthly to align harvest timing with the best‑priced market (Kanyakumari Uzhavar Sandhai).
